candidates.statement: In order to deal with such questions in the asymptotic region when $q\to\infty$ we should be more modest and ask questions of a more statistical flavor: what is the typical shape of a Young diagram contributing to a given representation? what are the fluctuations of the Young diagrams around the most probable shape?
Results presented in this article suggest that it should be possible to describe in this framework also the fluctuations of Young diagrams and we will deal with this problem in a forthcoming article.

Biane [@Biane2001approximate] proved (under some mild technical assumptions) that Young diagrams contributing to some finite-dimensional reducible representation of the symmetric group $S_q$ will concentrate around some limit shape if and only if the normalized character of the representation $$\chi(\pi):=\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\rho(\pi)}{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\rho(e)}$$ approximately factorizes, i.e. informally speaking $$\label{eq:approximate} \chi( \sigma_1 \cdots \sigma_n) \approx \chi(\sigma_1) \cdots \chi(\sigma_n)$$ for all permutations $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ with disjoint supports (to be more precise: we consider a sequence of representations $(\rho_q)$ where $\rho_q$ is a representation of $S_q$ and the approximate equality [\[eq:approximate\]](#eq:approximate){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:approximate"} should hold in the limit $q\to\infty$).

The result of Biane can be viewed as an analogue of the law of large numbers while the results presented in this article are an analogue of the central limit theorem; one can ask therefore which condition should replace [\[eq:approximate\]](#eq:approximate){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:approximate"} in order to prove such stronger results.

If we treat permutations $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ as random variables and the normalized character $\chi$ as an expectation ${\mathbb{E}}$ then this condition can be equivalently written as a condition for the covariance: $$\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)={\mathbb{E}}( \sigma_1 \sigma_2)-{\mathbb{E}}(\sigma_1) {\mathbb{E}}(\sigma_2) \approx 0.$$ Covariance is a special case of a more general probabilistic notion of a cumulant (we will recall the necessary definitions in Section [\[subsec:cumulants\]](#subsec:cumulants){reference-type="ref" reference="subsec:cumulants"}) therefore it is quite natural to expect that the correct condition for the factorization of characters should involve all cumulants and indeed in this article we prove that the following condition is sufficient for our purposes (Theorem and Definition [\[theo:main\]](#theo:main){reference-type="ref" reference="theo:main"}): for any cycles $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ with disjoint supports we assume that $$\label{eq:approximate2} k_n(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n) = O\big(q^{- \frac{|\sigma_1|+\cdots+|\sigma_n|+2(n-1)}{2} } \big),$$ where $|\pi|$ denotes the minimal number of factors needed to write the permutation $\pi$

It should be stressed that the decay of the cumulants in the condition [\[eq:approximate2\]](#eq:approximate2){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:approximate2"} carries a strong resemblance to the decay of the cumulants of the entries of many interesting classes of random matrices [@Collins2002] and, as we mentioned in Section [\[subsec:higherorder\]](#subsec:higherorder){reference-type="ref" reference="subsec:higherorder"}, it is not an accident.

Every finite-dimensional representation $\rho_q$ of the symmetric group $S_q$ defines a canonical probability measure on the Young diagrams contributing to $\rho_q$ given as follows: probability of a Young diagram $\lambda$ should be proportional to the total dimension of all irreducible components of type $[\lambda]$.

In principle, the information about the characters such as [\[eq:approximate2\]](#eq:approximate2){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:approximate2"} should be sufficient to compute the distribution of random variables $f(\lambda)$ for reasonable functions $f$, however this relation is not very direct.

An analogue of this situation can be found in the random matrix theory, where the knowledge of the joint distribution of the entries of a random matrix should be enough to find the joint distribution of the eigenvalues, however the actual calculation might be quite involved.

We can treat any commuting family of elements of the group algebra ${\mathbb{C}}(S_q)$ as a family of random variables equipped with the mean value given by the normalized character: $$\label{eq:wartoscoczekiwana} {\mathbb{E}}X:= \chi^{\rho_q}(X)= \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}} \rho_q(X)}{\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\rho_q(1)}.$$ It should be stressed that in the general case we treat elements of ${\mathbb{C}}(S_q)$ as random variables only on a purely formal level; in particular we do not treat them as functions on some Kolmogorov probability space.
